sketches.title: Spill to Scandal
sketches.premise: A drink hits the cruise-ship deck. Build the same chain of trouble, one link at a time: spill, reaction, cover-up, worse reaction. Make your partner responsible for the next mess. The ship will survive. Your dignity will not.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds exactly one believable next consequence to the whole chain; a skipped link jumps past a needed cause, an ending declares the trouble finished, and an undo cancels or rewrites an earlier link.
sketches.move_shape: Name one new consequence and make one player pay for it: “The rum reaches the captain’s shoes, so you hide the mop and blame my sea legs.”
sketches.first_card: The first drink spills beside the midnight buffet.

sketches.title: Deck by Deck
sketches.premise: Start with one spilled drink and move the same mess through the ship, one deck at a time. Each move must say where the mess goes next and what it picks up. Dry commentary is free; dry carpet is not.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it advances the mess to one connected next deck while carrying every object, person, and problem already aboard; a skipped link teleports it, an ending stops before the target deck, and an undo sends it back or removes a carried fact.
sketches.move_shape: Give the next deck and one new thing the mess catches: “On Deck 5, it soaks the karaoke list and gives the singer a tragic new verse.”
sketches.first_card: A blue cocktail spills outside the pool bar on Deck 10.

sketches.title: The Cruise Excuse
sketches.premise: A spilled drink starts an accusation. Build one shared excuse that grows detail by detail, but each detail must answer the last question raised by the ship’s staff. Your partner gets the blame, the terrible habit, or the bill. Try not to sound guilty; that would be ambitious.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it answers the current unanswered question and preserves every earlier fact; a skipped link answers a later question without closing the current one, an ending claims the excuse is accepted, and an undo denies a fact already used.
sketches.move_shape: Answer the next obvious question while costing your partner: “Who knocked it over? You did, while demonstrating a safety dance you invented.”
sketches.first_card: The purser points at the first spilled drink and asks, “Who was holding the glass?”

sketches.title: Ship of Blame
sketches.premise: A drink spills, and a ridiculous blame trail begins. Pass the blame from one person, object, or ship system to the next, one handoff at a time. Each handoff must leave the last blamed thing involved. Congratulations: you are building a ladder made of bad choices.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it names exactly one believable handoff that keeps the previous blamed thing connected to the mess; a skipped link jumps to an unrelated culprit, an ending names the final culprit and stops, and an undo clears or reverses a handoff already made.
sketches.move_shape: Make one handoff and leave the old culprit attached: “The glass blames your elbow, your elbow blames the wet napkin, and the napkin blames the ship’s fake palm tree.”
sketches.first_card: A waiter asks why the first drink is on the floor.

sketches.title: Captain Makes It Worse
sketches.premise: The first spilled drink triggers an official ship announcement. Build the same announcement one sentence at a time, with each new sentence making the problem clearer and the captain look worse. Your partner supplies the detail that turns routine news into public humiliation.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds one next sentence that follows from the entire announcement and raises the same trouble; a skipped link introduces a new crisis without a bridge, an ending gives the final announcement, and an undo retracts or changes a sentence already broadcast.
sketches.move_shape: Add one sentence that follows and stings: “Passengers are asked to avoid the wet floor; passengers are also asked to stop applauding the man who caused it.”
sketches.first_card: The captain announces that a drink has been spilled near the grand staircase.

sketches.title: The Wet-Floor Case
sketches.premise: Investigate one spilled drink by building the same chain of clues from the first puddle to the person who caused it. Add one clue at a time; every clue must connect to what is already known. Make your partner’s clue embarrassing, costly, or both. The truth may be ugly, but at least it will be organized.
sketches.criterion: A move HOLDS if it adds one checkable clue that follows from the full clue chain; a skipped link leaps over what the clue would establish, an ending names the culprit, and an undo removes or contradicts a clue already used.
sketches.move_shape: Add one clue and make it hurt: “The puddle contains glitter from your bargain hat, which is still stuck to the ceiling fan.”
sketches.first_card: A blue drink is found spilled beside a locked supply closet.
